name: trafilatura
purpose: Python library and CLI that downloads web pages and extracts the main text, metadata, comments and publication dates, stripping navigation and boilerplate, with output to text, XML, JSON and TEI.
journalism_use_case: The extraction layer under any news-monitoring or narrative-tracking pipeline: fetch thousands of articles from a list of outlets and get clean text plus a reliable publication date, which is what makes 'how did this claim propagate across these fifty sites' answerable at all.
pros: Publication-date extraction is the underrated feature and often the hardest part: narrative-propagation analysis is worthless without reliable dates, and trafilatura handles the messy real-world cases better than readability-style extractors
Benchmarked against competing extractors by its own maintainer with published methodology, so quality claims are traceable rather than asserted
Apache-2.0, actively maintained (v2.3.1, 2026-10-06; pushed 2026-11-17) with a clean tracker (57 open issues against 7,144 stars)
Pure Python with a CLI, so it works both in a pipeline and for one-off extraction, and runs anywhere including air-gapped
cons: Extraction is heuristic: unusual layouts, paywalled stubs and JavaScript-rendered articles produce partial or empty results, so a pipeline needs failure handling and spot-checking rather than blind trust
No JavaScript rendering, so dynamically loaded articles need a browser step (Playwright) before extraction
Comment extraction quality varies a lot by site, and comments are often where the interesting material is
It extracts; it does not crawl or schedule, so you still need Scrapy or a feed reader around it
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 7,144 stars with 57 open issues, release v2.3.1 (2026-10-06), pushed 2026-11-17, Apache-2.0. Notably, it is the maintained alternative to fhamborg/news-please, which this session confirmed is ARCHIVED (archived=true, last push 2026-04-14) despite still appearing in data-journalism recommendations.
assessment: Adopt it as your default article extractor — and specifically in place of news-please, which is archived and still widely recommended. For your profile the combination that works is a feed reader or sitemap crawl for discovery, trafilatura for extraction, and a stored raw copy alongside the extracted text so you can re-extract when the heuristics improve or a failure is discovered. Log extraction failures explicitly rather than letting empty strings into the corpus.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-17, latest release v2.3.1 (2026-10-06), 7,144 stars, 57 open issues. Same-day commits with a 2.x release line and a single engaged academic maintainer with a long track record.
licence_restrictions: None material. Extracted article text remains the publishers' copyright — a republication question, not a licence one.
costs: No fee. CPU-only and fast; negligible infrastructure for tens of thousands of articles. Estimate.
privacy: Fetches pages directly from your host, so target sites see your requests. Processing is local. For monitoring a hostile outlet, use a dedicated egress.
alternatives: mozilla/readability for a JavaScript-ecosystem extractor
news-please — AVOID, archived as of 2026-04-14
Playwright plus trafilatura where articles are JavaScript-rendered

name: news-please
purpose: Integrated news crawler and information extractor that discovers articles from sitemaps and RSS, extracts text, title, author and date, and stores results in files, Elasticsearch or a database.
journalism_use_case: Historically the one-step answer to building a news corpus: point it at a list of outlets and get structured articles without assembling a crawler and an extractor yourself. Still the design people reach for when asked to build a news-monitoring dataset.
pros: Integrated discovery plus extraction plus storage was genuinely convenient, which is why it became a standard recommendation in computational-journalism and media-research work
Apache-2.0 with CommonCrawl integration, so it could build historical corpora as well as monitor forward — a capability few alternatives match
Large community (2,493 stars) and an academic lineage with published use in media-research literature
cons: ARCHIVED: the GitHub API reports archived=true with the last push 2026-04-14, so it is read-only and will receive no fixes — a decisive fact that most of the material recommending it has not caught up with
News-site structures and sitemap conventions change continuously, so an archived news crawler degrades quickly and silently (fewer articles found, not visible errors)
No releases were ever published, so there is no version to pin even if you fork it
Scrapy-based with an ageing dependency chain that will become harder to install
feedback: No individual user reports verified. The decisive documented fact, established in this session: archived=true per the GitHub API on 2026-11-17, last push 2026-04-14, 2,493 stars, 10 open issues — recorded in sources/evidence/leads.md L10. This is a project still widely recommended in data-journalism teaching material that is now frozen.
assessment: Avoid for new deployment and flag it if you see it recommended — the archival is recent enough that it has not propagated into the guidance people follow. For your profile the replacement is straightforward and arguably better: Scrapy or a sitemap crawl for discovery, trafilatura for extraction, your own storage. That is a day's work and leaves you with maintained components. Keep news-please in the catalogue precisely so the archival is visible.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=true, pushed_at 2026-04-14, no releases, 2,493 stars, 10 open issues. Archived by the maintainer — unambiguous, and the single most consequential maintenance finding in the A1 segment given how widely the project is still recommended.
licence_restrictions: None, but the code is frozen. Forking is permitted and would be the only way forward.
costs: No fee. Not worth operating; any use means accepting fork-and-maintain responsibility.
privacy: Crawls target sites directly from your host; storage is local or your own Elasticsearch.
alternatives: trafilatura plus Scrapy — the recommended replacement, both actively maintained
Scrapy with a sitemap spider plus your own extraction
Media Cloud for an existing news archive rather than building your own
blockers: Archived as of 2026-04-14 — read-only, and news-site changes will silently degrade coverage

name: FreshRSS
purpose: Self-hosted feed aggregator supporting RSS, Atom and scraped sources, with multi-user accounts, filtering rules, full-text retrieval, labels and a REST API compatible with mobile readers.
journalism_use_case: The newsroom's monitoring backbone: hundreds of feeds — government press-release pages, court listings, regulatory bulletins, target company blogs, regional outlets — read in one place with filters that surface the handful of items that matter, and an API so a monitoring pipeline can consume the same stream.
pros: Self-hosted means your reading list — which is a map of your editorial interests — stays private, unlike a commercial reader where it is a product dataset
Filtering rules and labels make several hundred feeds manageable, which is the difference between a monitoring system and an unread inbox
REST API lets a pipeline consume the same curated stream reporters read, so monitoring and automation share one source of truth
AGPL-3.0, very actively maintained (1.30.4, 2026-10-21; pushed 2026-11-17) with a large community (16,610 stars)
cons: 680 open issues and a PHP application with a broad feature surface, so operating it means staying current with updates
Feed discovery is your problem: many government and corporate pages have no feed, so RSSHub or rss-bridge is needed alongside it
Full-text retrieval of articles whose feeds carry only excerpts works variably and can look like scraping to the publisher
Multi-user but not collaborative: there is no shared annotation or assignment, so turning an interesting item into newsroom action happens elsewhere
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 16,610 stars with 680 open issues, release 1.30.4 (2026-10-21), pushed 2026-11-17, AGPL-3.0. A long-established self-hosted reader with a large community; the issue count reflects feature breadth and user base.
assessment: Adopt it — a curated, self-hosted feed layer is the single highest-return piece of monitoring infrastructure a newsroom can run, and it costs almost nothing. For your profile the design that pays off is treating feeds as a shared asset: maintain the feed list in version control, use labels that map to beats, and expose the API to your own alerting so a reporter and a script see the same items. Pair with RSSHub for sources that lack feeds.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-17, latest release 1.30.4 (2026-10-21), 16,610 stars, 680 open issues. Same-day commits with a regular release cadence from an established community team.
licence_restrictions: AGPL-3.0: a modified instance offered to users obliges source publication. Running the release for your newsroom is unaffected.
costs: No fee. Infrastructure estimate: a small PHP host with a database — comfortably the cheapest substantial capability in this catalogue. Operating effort is low. Assumptions: a few hundred feeds, small team.
privacy: Self-hosted, so your feed list and reading behaviour stay internal. Your server fetches the feeds, so publishers see your server rather than individual reporters — an incidental privacy benefit.
alternatives: Miniflux for a lighter, more opinionated self-hosted reader
RSSHub or rss-bridge to generate feeds for sources that lack them
changedetection.io where the source has neither a feed nor a generator

name: Miniflux
purpose: Minimalist self-hosted feed reader written in Go, with a single binary, PostgreSQL storage, filtering rules, full-text extraction and a Google Reader-compatible API.
journalism_use_case: The same monitoring role as FreshRSS with a deliberately smaller surface: a single Go binary and a database, which suits an engineer who wants feed infrastructure that will keep working for years without attention.
pros: Single static binary plus PostgreSQL is about as low-maintenance as self-hosted infrastructure gets — a meaningful advantage when the alternative is another PHP application to patch
Opinionated minimalism means fewer features to misconfigure and a much smaller attack surface than a feature-rich reader
Apache-2.0 with consistent releases (2.3.5, 2026-11-02; pushed 2026-11-12) and a healthy tracker (290 open issues against 9,949 stars)
Google Reader-compatible API means existing mobile and desktop clients work, so reporters can use whatever reader they like
cons: Deliberately feature-light: no labels-and-rules sophistication to match FreshRSS, so managing several hundred feeds is less comfortable
Single-maintainer project, which for infrastructure you depend on for years is a real consideration even with the current good cadence
PostgreSQL requirement adds a stateful dependency that the single-binary story otherwise avoids
Same feed-discovery gap as any reader: sources without feeds need a generator
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 9,949 stars with 290 open issues, release 2.3.5 (2026-11-02), pushed 2026-11-12, Apache-2.0. Known in the self-hosting community specifically for its minimalism and stability.
assessment: A reasonable alternative to FreshRSS where you value operational simplicity over feature depth, which for an engineering-led team is a legitimate preference. For your profile I would choose FreshRSS if non-technical reporters will use the web interface and manage their own filters, and Miniflux if the reader is primarily a machine-readable monitoring substrate with reporters using their own clients. Either is better than none, and the choice is lower-stakes than it looks.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-12, latest release 2.3.5 (2026-11-02), 9,949 stars, 290 open issues. Regular releases from a single long-committed maintainer.
costs: No fee. A small VM plus PostgreSQL. The project also offers a paid hosted version — prices not verified here. Estimate.
privacy: Self-hosted; feed list and reading behaviour stay internal.
alternatives: FreshRSS for richer filtering and a reporter-facing interface
RSSHub for generating missing feeds
Commercial readers — avoid for monitoring, since the feed list reveals editorial interests

name: RSSHub
purpose: Extensible feed-generation service with several thousand community-maintained routes that produce RSS feeds for websites and platforms that provide none, including social platforms, forums and government sites.
journalism_use_case: Making unmonitorable sources monitorable: a ministry page with no feed, a regional forum, a company's announcements section, a social account — RSSHub generates a feed so your existing reader and alerting pipeline can watch it. This is what closes the gap between 'we should monitor that' and 'we do'.
pros: Route breadth is the asset: several thousand community routes mean the obscure source you need is often already covered, and writing a new route is modest work
Turns the feed reader you already run into a universal monitoring system, which is far cheaper than per-source change detection
Extremely active (release dated 2026-11-17 with same-day push, 47,071 stars) and an exceptionally low open-issue count for its size (25)
Self-hostable, so your monitored sources stay private and you are not rate-limited by a public instance
cons: Routes scrape third-party sites, so they break when sites change — with thousands of routes, some are always broken, and a silently broken route looks like 'no news' rather than an error
AGPL-3.0 network copyleft applies to a modified public instance, which matters if you offer feeds to partners
Scraping platforms may breach their terms of service, and for social platforms specifically the routes exist in a grey area that can stop working abruptly
Public instances see which sources you monitor, and are heavily rate-limited — self-hosting is effectively required for serious use
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 47,071 stars with only 25 open issues and a release on 2026-11-17 with same-day push, AGPL-3.0. The very low issue count against enormous scale suggests aggressive triage; route breakage is handled through continuous community contribution rather than issue accumulation.
assessment: Adopt and self-host — the combination of FreshRSS plus a private RSSHub covers an enormous share of newsroom monitoring need at almost no cost. For your profile the operational discipline that matters is detecting silent route failure: a monitoring system that quietly stops reporting is worse than none, so add a staleness check that alerts when a feed produces nothing for an unexpected period. Treat social-platform routes as fragile by nature.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-17, latest release v2026.11.17-8661.cf95739 published the same day, 47,071 stars, 25 open issues. Continuous-delivery release scheme with same-day commits and a very large contributor community.
model_or_data_licence: n/a. Content in generated feeds belongs to the source publishers.
licence_restrictions: AGPL-3.0: a modified instance served to others obliges source publication. Separately, individual routes may scrape sites whose terms prohibit it — a terms rather than licence question, and one worth considering per route.
costs: No fee. Infrastructure estimate: a small Node service; resource use scales with the number and frequency of routes you poll. Assumptions: self-hosted, moderate route count.
privacy: Self-hosting keeps your monitored-source list private, which matters because that list reveals your editorial interests. Your instance's requests are visible to the scraped sites.
alternatives: rss-bridge as an alternative feed generator with a different route set
changedetection.io for sources where no route exists and you only need change alerts
Direct API access where a source offers one

name: RSS-Bridge
purpose: PHP service with community-maintained 'bridges' that generate RSS, Atom and JSON feeds from websites and platforms lacking them.
journalism_use_case: The same gap-filling role as RSSHub, with a different bridge catalogue — so between the two, a source that neither covers is genuinely rare. Useful specifically where RSSHub lacks a route for a European or niche source that RSS-Bridge happens to support.
pros: Unlicense (public domain) — the most permissive licence in this subcategory, so there is no copyleft consideration at all when deploying or modifying it
Different bridge catalogue from RSSHub, so running both maximises source coverage for little extra cost
Simple PHP deployment that runs on modest shared hosting, lowering the barrier where container infrastructure is unavailable
Actively maintained (pushed 2026-11-15) with a substantial community (9,353 stars)
cons: Release cadence has lapsed: the latest release object dates from 2025-08-05 against current commits, so you track the default branch and have no pinnable version
Same structural fragility as all feed generators: bridges break when sites change, and 291 open issues largely reflect that churn
Smaller bridge catalogue than RSSHub, so it is a complement rather than a substitute
PHP deployment is a different operational idiom from a Node or Go stack, which adds a second thing to maintain if you also run RSSHub
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 9,353 stars with 291 open issues, latest release 2025-08-05 against a push on 2026-11-15, Unlicense. The release gap alongside current commits is visible in the API data and is the notable operational caveat.
assessment: Integrate it as a secondary feed generator where RSSHub has no route — the marginal cost is a small PHP container and the marginal coverage is real. For your profile the Unlicense is worth noting: it is the one tool in this segment you can modify and redistribute with no obligation whatsoever, which makes it a reasonable base if you ever want to build a newsroom-specific feed generator. Track the default branch and pin by commit.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-15, latest release dated 2025-08-05, 9,353 stars, 291 open issues. Commits are current; release engineering has lapsed, which is a pinning inconvenience rather than an activity concern.
model_or_data_licence: n/a. Feed content belongs to the source publishers.
licence_restrictions: None whatsoever — public-domain dedication. Bridges may scrape sites whose terms prohibit it, which is a separate consideration.
costs: No fee. A small PHP host; negligible.
privacy: Self-hosting keeps your monitored-source list private; your instance's requests are visible to scraped sites.
alternatives: RSSHub as the primary generator with a larger route catalogue
changedetection.io for change alerts where no feed can be generated
Writing a small bespoke scraper for a single critical source, which is often simpler than maintaining a bridge

name: feedparser
purpose: Python library that parses RSS, Atom and RDF feeds of any version, normalising their inconsistencies and handling malformed markup, date formats and character encodings.
journalism_use_case: The parsing layer in any custom monitoring pipeline: real-world feeds from government and regional sources are frequently malformed, use obsolete formats or carry broken date fields, and feedparser absorbs that mess so your code sees consistent records.
pros: Handles the pathological real-world feeds that a strict XML parser rejects — which is most government and small-publisher feeds, so this is where the practical value sits
Date normalisation across a dozen malformed conventions is work you would otherwise redo badly, and dates matter for monitoring
Licence resolved in this survey: BSD-2-Clause (GitHub reports NOASSERTION), actively maintained (v6.0.14, 2026-07-30; pushed 2026-11-02)
Two decades of accumulated edge-case handling with 2,458 stars; stable API so pipelines keep working
cons: GitHub reports SPDX NOASSERTION, so automated licence scanning does not resolve it — the BSD-2-Clause position comes from reading the repository and should be recorded explicitly
Parsing only: no fetching, scheduling, deduplication or storage, so it is one component among several
123 open issues on a mature library, mostly long-tail format edge cases
Feed parsing is a solved problem, so the library's ceiling is 'does not get in the way' rather than any differentiating capability
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 2,458 stars with 123 open issues, release v6.0.14 (2026-07-30), pushed 2026-11-02, SPDX NOASSERTION with the licence resolved to BSD-2-Clause — consistent with session 1's a1disc/notes.md, which independently recorded feedparser as BSD-2-Clause after reading the licence text.
assessment: Adopt it whenever you write feed-handling code rather than parsing XML yourself — the malformed-feed handling alone justifies it. For your profile this is uninteresting infrastructure that prevents a specific recurring bug: a monitoring job that silently drops items because one publisher emits a non-standard date. Record the BSD-2-Clause licence reference in your compliance notes given the SPDX gap.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-02, latest release v6.0.14 (2026-07-30), 2,458 stars, 123 open issues, SPDX NOASSERTION. Regular releases on a mature library from a committed maintainer.
licence: BSD-2-Clause (resolved by reading the repository licence; GitHub reports NOASSERTION — independently recorded in session 1's a1disc/notes.md)
privacy: Pure parsing; no network calls of its own.
alternatives: FreshRSS or Miniflux if you want a reader rather than a library
Direct XML parsing — not recommended, given real-world feed quality
trafilatura for article content once a feed gives you URLs

name: Playwright
purpose: Browser-automation framework driving Chromium, Firefox and WebKit with a unified API, auto-waiting, network interception, tracing and headless or headed operation.
journalism_use_case: Reaching the content that simple HTTP requests cannot: government portals behind JavaScript, dashboards that render client-side, document viewers that paginate via XHR, and forms that must be filled to produce a report. It is also the engine under browsertrix-crawler, shot-scraper and Crawlee.
pros: Network interception is the underused feature for investigative work: rather than scraping rendered HTML, you can capture the JSON API calls a dashboard makes and get structured data directly
Cross-browser support matters more than it sounds — some government portals work only in specific engines, and WebKit coverage occasionally rescues an otherwise inaccessible source
Apache-2.0 with exceptional maintenance (v1.65.1, 2026-11-13; pushed 2026-11-17) and only 71 open issues against 100,396 stars — outstanding triage at enormous scale
Tracing and video capture make a scraping run auditable, which is useful when you need to show how data was obtained
cons: Resource-heavy relative to HTTP scraping: each browser instance costs hundreds of megabytes, so large crawls need orchestration and patience
Browser automation is detectable, and portals increasingly block it — so you may win access and lose it again, which makes a brittle dependency for ongoing monitoring
Browser binaries are large downloads tied to Playwright versions, which complicates air-gapped and reproducible deployments
General-purpose: it is included here for the concrete journalism use case, but most of its documentation and community are about software testing
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 100,396 stars with 71 open issues, release v1.65.1 (2026-11-13), pushed 2026-11-17, Apache-2.0. Its role in journalism tooling is verifiable from dependency relationships: browsertrix-crawler, shot-scraper and Crawlee all build on it.
assessment: Adopt it for the specific cases that defeat plain HTTP, and resist using it where requests would do — the resource and brittleness costs are real. For your profile the highest-leverage technique is network interception: find the underlying API call a portal makes, then call that directly without the browser, which is faster, more stable and often yields cleaner data than the rendered page. Use Playwright to discover the API, not necessarily to run the collection.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-17, latest release v1.65.1 (2026-11-13), 100,396 stars, 71 open issues. Same-day commits, near-weekly releases, corporate backing, and an exceptionally low backlog for the scale.
licence_restrictions: None material. Note that automating access to a site may breach its terms of service — separate from the licence.
costs: No fee. Infrastructure: browser instances are memory-hungry (budget several hundred MB each) plus disk for browser binaries. For large crawls this is the dominant cost. Estimate.
privacy: Requests originate from your host, so targets see your IP and an automatable browser fingerprint. Processing is local. Use a dedicated egress for sensitive targets.
alternatives: Direct HTTP requests to the underlying API once discovered — faster and more stable
Crawlee for a crawling framework that wraps Playwright with queueing and anti-blocking
Puppeteer for a Chromium-only alternative

name: MarkItDown
purpose: Python utility that converts many file and document formats — Office documents, PDFs, HTML, images, audio, archives — into Markdown suitable for text processing and language-model input.
journalism_use_case: Fast, uniform conversion of a mixed document set into readable Markdown for triage and search: a folder containing Word files, spreadsheets, PDFs and web captures becomes one consistent text corpus in a single command, which is often all you need before deciding what deserves careful extraction.
pros: Format breadth with almost no configuration: for quick triage of a heterogeneous dump it is the lowest-effort option in this catalogue
MIT licensed with enormous adoption (195,958 stars) and active maintenance (v0.1.9, 2026-10-21; pushed 2026-11-07)
Markdown output is both human-readable and well-suited to downstream search or model input, so one conversion serves several purposes
Simple enough to drop into a pipeline in minutes, which matters when a document set arrives at short notice
cons: Conversion fidelity is shallow compared with Docling or Marker: layout, reading order and table structure are not properly modelled, so complex documents lose structure silently
818 open issues against a very fast-growing project — expect rough edges and API churn, and pin the version
Designed primarily to feed language models, so defaults optimise for 'text a model can read' rather than for evidentiary fidelity, and the distinction matters when an extraction may be quoted
Some converters may invoke external services or models depending on configuration, which needs checking before running it on sensitive material
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 195,958 stars with 818 open issues, release v0.1.9 (2026-10-21), pushed 2026-11-07, MIT licence. The scale of adoption is clear; the issue count reflects very rapid growth rather than neglect.
assessment: Use it for triage and not for evidence. The honest division for your profile is: MarkItDown to see what is in a folder quickly, Docling or Marker for documents whose structure matters and whose extraction may be quoted, and the original file always retained. Check the configuration before running it on source material, since some conversion paths can reach for external services, and that would be an unacceptable disclosure for leaked documents.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-07, latest release v0.1.9 (2026-10-21), 195,958 stars, 818 open issues. Current commits and releases under corporate maintenance; the enormous backlog is a function of explosive adoption.
model_or_data_licence: n/a for the core; optional model-based converters depend on whatever model you configure.
licence_restrictions: Code unrestricted. Verify the licence of any model-based converter you enable.
costs: No fee. CPU-light for most formats. If model-based conversion paths are enabled, those costs apply (not priced here).
privacy: Local for the standard converters. The item to verify is whether any enabled converter calls an external service — check before processing source documents.
alternatives: Docling for layout-aware, provenance-preserving conversion
Apache Tika for maximum format coverage with metadata
Marker where conversion accuracy is the priority and the weights licence is acceptable
